heath_proof: For let the area ABCD be contained by the rational straight line AB and the sixth binomial AD, divided into its terms at E, so that AE is the greater term; I say that the “side” of AC is the side of the sum of two medial areas. Let the same construction be made as before shown. It is then manifest that MO is the “side” of AC, and that MN is incommensurable in square with NO. Now, since EA is incommensurable in length with AB, therefore EA, AB are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore AK, that is, the sum of the squares on MN, NO, is medial. [X. 21] Again, since ED is incommensurable in length with AB, therefore FE is also incommensurable with EK; [X. 13] therefore FE, EK are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore EL, that is, MR, that is, the rectangle MN, NO, is medial. [X. 21] And, since AE is incommensurable with EF, AK is also incommensurable with EL. [VI. 1, X. 11] But AK is the sum of the squares on MN, NO, and EL is the rectangle MN, NO; therefore the sum of the squares on MN, NO is incommensurable with the rectangle MN, NO. And each of them is medial, and MN, NO are incommensurable in square. Therefore MO is the side of the sum of two medial areas [X. 41], and is the “side” of AC.

10.59
**Statement:** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and the sixth binomial, the âsideâ of the area is the irrational straight line called the side of the sum of two medial areas.

**Step 1.** Let the area ABCD be contained by the rational straight line AB and the sixth binomial straight line AD, and let AD be divided into its terms at E, where AE is the greater term. We must show that the "side" of the area ABCD is the side of the sum of two medial areas.

**Step 2.** Since AD is a sixth binomial, by the definition of a sixth binomial (D10.2.6), neither AE nor ED is commensurable in length with the rational straight line set out, and the square on AE is greater than the square on ED by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AE.

**Step 3.** Let the rational straight line AB be the assigned rational straight line. Since AD is a sixth binomial, AE and ED are rational straight lines commensurable in square only (by the definition of a binomial, 10.36), neither AE nor ED is commensurable in length with AB, and the square on AE exceeds the square on ED by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AE.

**Step 4.** Bisect ED at the point F, so that EF = FD [by 1.10]. Apply to AE a rectangle equal to the square on EF and deficient by a square figure, producing the rectangle AG·GE [by 6.28]. Since the square on AE is greater than the square on ED by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AE, and the rectangle applied to AE equals the fourth part of the square on ED (since EF is half of ED, so the square on EF is one-fourth the square on ED), by 10.18, AG is incommensurable in length with GE.

**Step 5.** Since AG is incommensurable in length with GE, the rectangle AG·GE is incommensurable with the squares on AG and GE individually. But the rectangle AE·ED = the rectangle AG·GE taken together with appropriate terms from the identity on the bisection. Now, since AE and ED are rational and commensurable in square only, the rectangle AE·ED is medial [by 10.21].

**Step 6.** Since neither AE nor ED is commensurable in length with AB, and AE, ED are rational, the squares on AE and on ED are each incommensurable with the square on AB. Thus the square on AE is medial relative to AB, and similarly the square on ED is medial relative to AB [by D10.1.4 and 10.22, since a rational line incommensurable in length with AB produces a medial square relative to AB].

**Step 7.** Now let the rectangle AB·AE equal the square on H, and let the rectangle AB·ED equal the square on K, for some straight lines H and K [constructing squares equal to these rectangles by 2.14].

**Step 8.** Since AE is incommensurable in length with AB, the rectangle AB·AE is irrational, meaning that the square on H is irrational, so H is irrational [by 10.21 and D10.1.4]. Similarly, since ED is incommensurable in length with AB, the rectangle AB·ED is irrational, so K is irrational.

**Step 9.** Since AE is incommensurable in length with ED (as they are commensurable in square only), and AB·AE : AB·ED = AE : ED [by 6.1], the rectangle AB·AE is incommensurable with the rectangle AB·ED [by 10.11]. Therefore the square on H is incommensurable with the square on K, so H and K are incommensurable in square.

**Step 10.** Now consider the sum of the squares on H and K. We have the square on H + the square on K = AB·AE + AB·ED = AB·(AE + ED) = AB·AD [by 2.1]. Since AD is a sixth binomial and neither of its terms is commensurable in length with AB, the square on AE is incommensurable with the rectangle AB·AE, and the area AB·AD contains both medial and irrational components. More precisely, the square on H equals AB·AE, and AE is rational but incommensurable in length with AB, so the square on H (= AB·AE) is medial [by 10.21]. Similarly the square on K (= AB·ED) is medial. Therefore the sum of the squares on H and K is the sum of two medial areas.

**Step 11.** We must show this sum is itself medial. The square on H = AB·AE is medial, and the square on K = AB·ED is medial. Now AE : ED is not a ratio of number to number (since AE and ED are incommensurable in length), so AB·AE is incommensurable with AB·ED [by 10.11]. Thus the sum of the squares on H and K is the sum of two incommensurable medial areas, which makes the sum medial [since each is medial and they are incommensurable, their sum is medial by 10.15 applied inversely -- actually their sum is irrational; it is medial only if commensurable with a medial, but in fact the sum of two incommensurable medials is in general not medial but rather an irrational area].

**Step 12.** Let us reconsider more carefully following the structure of 10.57 and 10.58. Apply to AB the areas: let AB·AE = square on some line, and AB·ED = square on some line. Instead, following the standard construction, let us find the "side" of the rectangle AB·AD directly.

**Step 13.** Set out the rational straight line AB, and the sixth binomial AD divided at E with AE > ED. Bisect ED at F. Apply to AE a parallelogram equal to the square on EF, deficient by a square, producing the rectangle on AG, GE [by 6.28]. Then AG is incommensurable in length with GE [by 10.18, since sq(AE) > sq(ED) by the square on a line incommensurable with AE].

**Step 14.** Construct: let the square on H equal the rectangle AB·AG, and the square on K equal the rectangle AB·GE [by 2.14, constructing H and K as the mean proportionals, i.e., AB : H = H : AG and AB : K = K : GE, using 6.13].

**Step 15.** Since AG + GE = AE, we have AB·AG + AB·GE = AB·AE [by 2.1], so the square on H + the square on K = AB·AE.

**Step 16.** Now, AG is incommensurable in length with GE [Step 4]. Since AB is rational, and AG, GE are parts of AE which is rational, AG and GE are rational. But AG is incommensurable in length with GE, so the rectangle AG·GE is medial [by 10.21].

**Step 17.** The rectangle AB·AG : AB·GE = AG : GE [by 6.1], and since AG is incommensurable in length with GE, the rectangle AB·AG is incommensurable with AB·GE [by 10.11]. Therefore the square on H is incommensurable with the square on K, so H is incommensurable in square with K.

**Step 18.** Since AE is incommensurable in length with AB [given, since AD is a sixth binomial], and AE = AG + GE, we need to examine whether AG or GE is commensurable with AB. Since neither AE nor ED is commensurable in length with AB, and AG, GE are obtained from subdividing AE by the application construction, neither AG nor GE is commensurable in length with AB.

**Step 19.** Since AG is incommensurable in length with AB, the rectangle AB·AG is irrational (not rational) [it cannot be expressed as a rational area]. More precisely, AB is rational and AG is rational but incommensurable in length with AB, so the rectangle AB·AG is medial [by 10.21]. Thus the square on H is medial, so H is a medial straight line [by D10.1.4 and 10.23].

**Step 20.** Similarly, since GE is incommensurable in length with AB, the rectangle AB·GE is medial [by 10.21]. Thus the square on K is medial, so K is medial.

**Step 21.** Therefore the squares on H and K are each medial, and by Step 17 they are incommensurable with each other. Hence the sum of the squares on H and K (= AB·AE) is the sum of two incommensurable medial areas. In particular, this sum is medial (as AB·AE is medial by 10.21, since AE is incommensurable in length with AB).

**Step 22.** Now consider twice the rectangle H·K. We have (H + K)^2 = sq(H) + sq(K) + 2·rect(H,K). Also, the rectangle AB·AD = AB·(AE + ED) = AB·AE + AB·ED = [sq(H) + sq(K)] + AB·ED [by 2.1 and Step 15]. We need to show that 2·rect(H,K) = AB·ED. 

**Step 23.** By the construction in Steps 13-14, AG·GE = EF^2 (from the application in Step 13). Also, AE·ED = AE·(2·EF) = 2·AE·EF. We have sq(H) = AB·AG and sq(K) = AB·GE. Then sq(H)·sq(K) = AB^2·AG·GE [by 6.16]. So rect(H,K)^2 = AB^2·AG·GE. Also, rect(H,K) = AB·sqrt(AG·GE). Since AG·GE = EF^2 [from the application], rect(H,K) = AB·EF.

**Step 24.** Therefore 2·rect(H,K) = 2·AB·EF = AB·(2·EF) = AB·ED [since ED = 2·EF by the bisection in Step 4].

**Step 25.** Now we must show that 2·rect(H,K) is medial. We have 2·rect(H,K) = AB·ED. Since ED is rational but incommensurable in length with AB [given for the sixth binomial], the rectangle AB·ED is medial [by 10.21]. So 2·rect(H,K) is medial.

**Step 26.** We must show that 2·rect(H,K) is incommensurable with the sum sq(H) + sq(K). We have sq(H) + sq(K) = AB·AE and 2·rect(H,K) = AB·ED. Now AB·AE : AB·ED = AE : ED [by 6.1]. Since AE and ED are commensurable in square only (incommensurable in length), AE : ED is not a ratio of number to number [by 10.7], so AB·AE is incommensurable with AB·ED [by 10.11]. Therefore sq(H) + sq(K) is incommensurable with 2·rect(H,K).

**Step 27.** Collecting the results: H and K are incommensurable in square [Step 17]; the sum of the squares on H and K is medial [Step 21]; twice the rectangle contained by H and K is medial [Step 25]; and the sum of the squares on them is incommensurable with twice the rectangle contained by them [Step 26].

**Step 28.** Therefore, by 10.41, the straight line H + K is the irrational line called the side of the sum of two medial areas.

**Step 29.** Now, sq(H + K) = sq(H) + sq(K) + 2·rect(H,K) = AB·AE + AB·ED = AB·AD [by Steps 15, 24, and 2.1]. Therefore H + K is the "side" of the area AB·AD, that is, the "side" of the area contained by the rational straight line AB and the sixth binomial AD.

**Step 30.** Therefore, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and the sixth binomial, the "side" of the area is the irrational straight line called the side of the sum of two medial areas. Q.E.D.
